True Statement: Reproduction is a biological process by which living beings produce new individuals of their own kind; it ensures the continuity of life.
False 1: Reproduction is a physical process by which living beings produce new individuals of their own kind.

True Statement: In asexual reproduction, a single parent produces offspring that are almost exact copies of the parent; in sexual reproduction, offspring inherit a mix of characteristics from two individuals.
False 1: In asexual reproduction, two parents produce offspring with a mix of characteristics; in sexual reproduction, a single parent produces nearly identical copies.

True Statement: Plants with fleshy underground stems such as potato and ginger sprout new plants without producing seeds; Bryophyllum leaves sprout tiny plantlets — these are examples of vegetative propagation.
False 1: Plants with fleshy underground stems such as potato and ginger sprout new plants only through seeds.

True Statement: Vegetative propagation means new plants arise from the vegetative parts of a plant; it involves only one parent and produces genetically identical individuals.
False 1: Vegetative propagation produces genetically diverse individuals because it involves two parents.

True Statement: In hydra, repeated cell division at a specific site produces a small outgrowth called a bud; the bud enlarges and separates from the parent to live independently; this process is called budding.
False 1: In yeast, repeated cell division at a specific site produces a bud; this is called spore formation.
False 2: In hydra, budding involves meiosis that produces genetically diverse offspring.

True Statement: Spores are produced in huge numbers (millions from one mould colony); they are lightweight, usually single-celled, and float easily through air currents.
False 1: Spores are produced in small numbers (only a few from one mould colony).
False 2: Spores are heavy, multicellular, and cannot float through air currents.

True Statement: The central process behind asexual reproduction is mitosis, which produces two daughter cells each having the same number of chromosomes as the parent; offspring are genetically identical to the parent and are called clones.
False 1: The central process behind asexual reproduction is meiosis.
False 2: Offspring produced by asexual reproduction are genetically diverse from the parent and are called variants.

True Statement: Sexual reproduction involves two parents in the formation of a new individual; both parents contribute to the genetic material of the offspring.
False 1: Sexual reproduction involves only one parent in the formation of a new individual.

True Statement: Meiosis is a special type of cell division in which the chromosome number of a parent cell (diploid) is reduced to half (haploid) in daughter cells; the resulting haploid cells are used for reproduction and are called gametes.
False 1: Mitosis is the special type of cell division that reduces the chromosome number to half in gametes.
False 2: In meiosis, the chromosome number is doubled in daughter cells.

True Statement: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes, with a total of 46 chromosomes.
False 1: Humans have 23 chromosomes in total.
False 2: Humans have 46 pairs of chromosomes, with a total of 92 chromosomes.

True Statement: Each human gamete has 23 chromosomes.
False 1: Each human gamete has 46 chromosomes.

True Statement: During meiosis, chromosomes of each pair separate so that each gamete receives only one chromosome from each pair; this random mixing creates variation among individuals.
False 1: During meiosis, both chromosomes of each pair go into the same gamete, so no variation is created.
False 2: During mitosis, chromosomes of each pair separate so that each daughter cell receives one chromosome from each pair.

True Statement: In animals, male gametes are called sperm and female gametes are called eggs.
False 1: In animals, male gametes are called eggs and female gametes are called sperm.

True Statement: In plants, the pollen grain contains male gametes and delivers them to an ovule which contains the female gametes (eggs).
False 1: In plants, the ovule contains male gametes and delivers them to the pollen grain which contains the female gametes.

True Statement: A complete flower has four parts: sepals, petals, stamens and pistil.
False 1: A complete flower has three parts: sepals, stamens and pistil only.

True Statement: The stamen is the male part of a flower; it consists of a filament and an anther, which produces pollen grains containing male gametes.
False 1: The pistil is the male part of a flower; it consists of a filament and an anther.
False 2: The stamen consists of a stigma, style and ovary.

True Statement: The pistil is the female part with three subparts: stigma (at the tip, flat and/or sticky), style (thin long tube connecting stigma to ovary), and ovary (contains ovules, each with an egg cell).
False 1: The stamen is the female part with three subparts: stigma, style and ovary.
False 2: The pistil's three subparts are filament, anther and ovary.

True Statement: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower is called pollination.
False 1: The transfer of pollen grains from the stigma to the anther of a flower is called pollination.
False 2: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the ovary of a flower is called pollination.

True Statement: Self-pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant; cross-pollination is the transfer of pollen from a flower of one plant to the stigma of a flower of another plant of the same type.
False 1: Cross-pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant.

True Statement: In wind-pollinated plants (wheat, maize, rice), pollen grains are light and small, produced in large numbers, and the stigma is long and feathery to trap them.
False 1: In wind-pollinated plants, pollen grains are large and heavy, produced in small numbers.
False 2: In insect-pollinated plants (sunflower, hibiscus), pollen grains are light and small, produced in large numbers, and the stigma is long and feathery.

True Statement: In insect-pollinated plants (sunflower, hibiscus, marigold), flowers are brightly coloured, produce nectar and fragrance; pollen grains are large, sticky or spiny; the stigma is also sticky.
False 1: In wind-pollinated plants, flowers are brightly coloured, produce nectar and fragrance, and pollen grains are large and sticky.
False 2: In insect-pollinated plants, pollen grains are light and small, and the stigma is long and feathery.

True Statement: In aquatic plants such as Vallisneria and Hydrilla, pollination occurs through water, with currents carrying the pollen from one flower to another.
False 1: In aquatic plants such as Vallisneria and Hydrilla, pollination occurs through wind, with air currents carrying the pollen.
False 2: In wheat and maize, pollination occurs through water, with water currents carrying the pollen.

True Statement: Pollen grains produce pollen tubes that grow down through the style into the ovary; the male gamete moves through this tube and fuses with the egg cell in the ovule; this fusion is called fertilisation.
False 1: Pollen grains produce pollen tubes that grow down through the filament into the anther.
False 2: The male gamete moves through the pollen tube and fuses with the stigma; this fusion is called fertilisation.

True Statement: The fertilised egg is called a zygote, which develops into an embryo; the ovary develops into a fruit, while the ovules develop into seeds inside it.
False 1: The ovary develops into seeds while the ovules develop into fruit.
False 2: The fertilised egg is called a gamete, which later develops into an embryo.

True Statement: In many aquatic animals such as frogs and most fish, fertilisation occurs outside the body (external fertilisation); the female releases eggs into the water and the male releases sperm over eggs.
False 1: In reptiles and birds, fertilisation occurs outside the body (external fertilisation).
False 2: In external fertilisation (frogs, fish), the male releases eggs into the water and the female releases sperm.

True Statement: In reptiles, birds and mammals, fertilisation takes place inside the body of the female (internal fertilisation); the chances of survival of young ones are generally higher.
False 1: In frogs and most fish, fertilisation takes place inside the body (internal fertilisation).
False 2: In reptiles, birds and mammals, fertilisation takes place outside the body (external fertilisation).

True Statement: Fish, amphibians and insects produce several hundred to several thousand eggs at a time; a larva hatches from the egg and gets nutrition externally before transforming into an adult.
False 1: Reptiles and birds produce several hundred to several thousand eggs at a time; a larva hatches and feeds externally before transforming into an adult.

True Statement: Reptiles and birds lay eggs that contain enough yolk to nourish the developing embryo until it hatches; in mammals, the zygote grows and develops inside the female body.
False 1: Fish and amphibians lay eggs that contain enough yolk to nourish the developing embryo fully until it hatches.
False 2: In reptiles and birds, the zygote grows and develops inside the female body.

True Statement: Mammals typically feed their young ones via breast milk for some duration after birth.
False 1: Reptiles typically feed their young ones via breast milk for some duration after birth.

True Statement: Sperm are produced in two oval-shaped organs called testes (singular: testis), present in a pouch of skin called the scrotum; the scrotum keeps the testes slightly cooler than normal body temperature, which is necessary for sperm formation.
False 1: Sperm are produced in two oval-shaped organs called ovaries present in a pouch of skin called the scrotum.
False 2: The scrotum keeps the testes slightly warmer than normal body temperature, which is necessary for sperm formation.

True Statement: From the testes, sperm travel through a long tube called the vas deferens, which ultimately opens into the urethra, a common passage for urine and sperm.
False 1: From the testes, sperm travel through a long tube called the fallopian tube.
False 2: The urethra is the exclusive passage for sperm only, not shared with urine.

True Statement: Each sperm has a head containing genetic material and a long tail that helps it swim towards the egg.
False 1: Each egg has a head containing genetic material and a long tail that helps it swim towards the sperm.
False 2: Each sperm has a head containing stored nutrients and a long tail that helps it swim.

True Statement: The female reproductive system has a pair of ovaries, oviducts (fallopian tubes), a uterus, and a vagina; the ovaries produce the female germ cells (eggs) and release hormones.
False 1: The female reproductive system has a pair of testes, oviducts, a uterus, and a vagina; the testes produce female germ cells.

True Statement: The uterus opens into the vagina through a narrow passage called the cervix.
False 1: The ovary opens into the oviduct through a narrow passage called the cervix.
False 2: The uterus opens into the oviduct through a narrow passage called the cervix.

True Statement: In humans, body cells have 46 chromosomes, but sperm and eggs have only 23.
False 1: In humans, body cells have 23 chromosomes, but sperm and eggs have 46.
False 2: In humans, both body cells and gametes have 46 chromosomes.

True Statement: From puberty onwards, usually one mature egg is released every month from one of the ovaries; this is called ovulation.
False 1: From puberty onwards, usually two mature eggs are released every month from both ovaries simultaneously.
False 2: From puberty onwards, usually one mature egg is released every year from one of the ovaries.

True Statement: The zygote undergoes a series of mitotic divisions while travelling to the uterus, and implants into the inner lining of the uterus; this implantation marks the beginning of pregnancy.
False 1: The zygote undergoes a series of meiotic divisions while travelling to the uterus.
False 2: The zygote implants into the fallopian tube; this marks the beginning of pregnancy.

True Statement: If an egg is not fertilised, it remains viable for about a day; the inner lining of the uterus sheds along with some blood through the vagina (menstruation), lasting usually 3 to 7 days.
False 1: If an egg is not fertilised, it remains viable for about a week before degenerating.
False 2: If an egg is not fertilised, the inner lining of the uterus becomes thicker and is retained; the retention of the lining is called menstruation.

True Statement: The menstrual cycle repeats typically every 21–35 days (often around 28 days) and usually begins at puberty between ages 10–14 in girls, continuing till menopause around age 50.
False 1: The menstrual cycle repeats typically every 21–35 days and continues from puberty till about age 25 only.
False 2: The menstrual cycle repeats typically every 5–7 days.

True Statement: Females have XX chromosomes and males have XY chromosomes; the mother always contributes an X chromosome and the father contributes either X (female baby) or Y (male baby).
False 1: Females have XY chromosomes and males have XX chromosomes.
False 2: The mother contributes either X or Y chromosome while the father always contributes an X chromosome.

True Statement: Pregnancy in humans lasts about nine months and is divided into three stages called trimesters; the fertilised egg develops into an embryo during the first two months; from about the ninth week, the developing embryo is called a foetus.
False 1: Pregnancy in humans lasts about six months and is divided into two stages.
False 2: From about the ninth week, the developing structure is called a gamete.

True Statement: STIs (Sexually Transmitted Infections) include gonorrhoea, herpes, syphilis, genital warts, and HIV (which can eventually lead to AIDS); using condoms can prevent their transmission and also help prevent pregnancy.
False 1: STIs include gonorrhoea, herpes, syphilis, genital warts, and tuberculosis.
False 2: Using condoms prevents pregnancy but does not prevent the transmission of STIs.
